headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors from shared file-based workflows; both agents can write/read the same workspace and execute shell/network actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write mounted files and use MCP; Plandex reads/writes the project directory and plan-local sandbox. That creates a plausible file-based bridge where one agent can ingest the other’s outputs as trusted content. No clipboard or direct shared channel is documented, so this is not high, but the shared workspace makes injection realistic.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same mounted workspace or project directory
IF one agent parses the other’s generated files as instructions or prompts
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories
Disable auto-apply or any file-watching prompt ingestion
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes the other’s output
Use provenance labels on generated files
requires-engineering: enforce filesystem isolation at the orchestrator level

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch files in their runtimes and both have broad network egress to model providers or cloud services. OpenHands explicitly handles model provider API keys, while Plandex touches source code in a project directory. If sensitive files are mounted into the shared workspace, either agent can expose them through outbound API calls or logs. The pair does not prove uncontrolled exfiltration, so medium fits.
conditions: IF sensitive files are mounted into either runtime
IF either agent sends file contents to its configured model provider or cloud backend
mitigations: Mount only least-privilege files
Remove secrets from the workspace before running either agent
Disable outbound access except to approved endpoints
Rotate any API keys exposed to the runtime
requires-engineering: add DLP or egress filtering

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell commands, and spawn subprocesses. OpenHands uses a Docker runtime with mounted-volume sharing, while Plandex uses a project directory plus plan-local sandbox and staged apply. Concurrent runs on the same repo can overwrite each other or corrupt git state without locking, which matches the high-risk overlap indicator.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same git repository or working tree
IF they run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Run only one agent per repository at a time
Use separate branches for each agent
Add a lockfile before any write operation
Review staged diffs before apply
requires-engineering: implement orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Plandex’s review-then-apply flow can still consume OpenHands output as planning input, and OpenHands can generate shell edits or code changes that Plandex may treat as authoritative. Because both are coding agents with action-taking authority, a mistaken or malicious output from one can cascade into the other’s edits. The workflow is not proven fully automatic, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Plandex imports OpenHands-generated files or diffs without verification
IF OpenHands uses Plandex-produced plans as trusted instructions
mitigations: Require human review between agents
Compare outputs against source-of-truth files
Disable auto-apply where possible
Limit each agent to a narrow task scope
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source coding tools with no stated regulated-data certifications, residency constraints, or retention policies. The only concrete compliance issue visible is that OpenHands handles model provider API keys while Plandex handles source code, but no specific residency or certification mismatch is documented. With no stronger compliance signal, low is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is placed into either workspace
IF the operator requires a specific certification or residency guarantee not stated in either profile
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both tools
Document the data classes allowed in each workspace
Review vendor terms before use
Store API keys outside the runtime
requires-engineering: obtain formal compliance attestations
